title: Pauri 1, meaning: joy, mother
hook: joy, mother, I have found the True Guru, easily, and the songs of joy are sung (Anand 1)
tomorrow: Stay with the Lord, my mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri one, satguroo, and your line, anand bhaiaa. Today, the same pauri, opened up for its meaning.

A baby is born in a Punjabi family, and within the hour the phone is ringing. Then the doorbell. Aunties arrive with sweets. Uncles arrive with more sweets. Someone puts music on. Everyone keeps saying one word to the parents, the grandparents, anyone standing still long enough: vadhaiyan! Congratulations! It's the word for news so good the whole family turns up. The first pauri of Anand Sahib has that word in it: a party in five lines, and the guests are not who you'd expect.
screen: `A BABY IS BORN; THE PHONE RINGS.` → `AUNTIES, SWEETS, MUSIC.` → `VADHAIYAN! CONGRATULATIONS!`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri, in paraphrase. Joy has come, my mother, for I have found the True Guru. I found the True Guru with ease, and my mind rings with congratulations. The jewel-like ragas, with their families, have come to sing the Word. Sing the Word of the Lord, all you who have set it in your minds. Says Nanak, bliss has come; I have found the True Guru. Take the pieces. First, mother: the news goes to the person you'd tell first. Then sahaj, with ease. Sahaj is a big word in Sikh thought: a natural, settled ease, the opposite of straining. The Guru wasn't won by force; the joy came the way sleep comes. Then the party. Vaadhaaeeaa, congratulations, the same word aunties call out at a birth. And who shows up? The ragas. In old Indian music lore, ragas were pictured with families and companions, so the pauri pictures the musical modes themselves arriving at the door like relatives, ready to sing: joy so big the music turns up in person. Then a turn outward: sing the Word, all of you who've taken it in. The joy doesn't stay private. Notice what this pauri isn't. It isn't a lecture about joy. It's a report of joy, from inside it, still breathless. That's what Guru Amar Das gives Sikhs to sing at the close of their gatherings: not an idea about bliss, but good news.
screen: `JOY HAS COME, MY MOTHER.` · `SAHAJ: FOUND WITH EASE.` · `THE RAGAS ARRIVE LIKE FAMILY.` · `SING THE WORD, ALL OF YOU.` · then, large: `JOY, MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go over the last few days and find one piece of good news, any size: a friend's recovery, a finished project, a small win nobody noticed. Feel it again from inside, the way the pauri does, as news worth carrying to the first person you'd tell. If you pray, you can thank the Guru with Waheguru.
Sahaj, natural ease. Joy has come, my mother: the Guru found with sahaj, the mind ringing with congratulations, and the ragas arriving like family to sing.
Your line: joy, mother. Some news is too good to keep in one room. Three hundred eighty-two days, and counting.

screen: `DAY 382 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: STAY WITH THE LORD, MY MIND.`

howItsDone: The first pauri of Anand Sahib is sung at the close of Sikh gatherings, from weddings to ordinary services.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about feeling happy.
what it means: a breathless report of joy: the Guru found with ease, congratulations ringing, the ragas arriving to sing, and an invitation to everyone.
what a scholar hears: 'raag ratan parvaar pareeaa' draws on the old Indian picture of ragas with families of raginis and companions, here gathering as at a birth.

chat.says: Anand Sahib begins with 'joy has come.' How did it come? Through really hard work?
options: With sahaj, ease: the Guru was found naturally, the way sleep comes, not by force.
Through years of strict effort that finally forced the door to open wide.
By luck alone; the pauri says the singer just happened to be nearby.
chat.meaning: The pauri says the True Guru was found with sahaj, a natural, settled ease, the opposite of straining.

notes: Pauri 1 paraphrased in full ('satgur ta paaiaa sahaj setee man vajeeaa vaadhaaeeaa; raag ratan parvaar pareeaa sabad gaavan aaeeaa; sabado ta gaavahu haree keraa man jinee vasaaiaa'). Confirm.
Vaadhaaeeaa linked to the modern Punjabi 'vadhaiyan' (congratulations). Confirm.
Reading of 'parvaar pareeaa' as the ragas' families/companions (raginis); some commentators read pareeaa as fairies or consorts. Confirm.
Day 133 already used the 'mother / kitchen door' image; today's angle is congratulations and the ragas arriving.
